slides.1.title: The Portuguese Wine Classification Pyramid
slides.1.html:
Portugal's classification system is aligned with EU rules and has three main tiers:

🥇 DOC (Denominação de Origem Controlada) = DOP

  • The highest tier, equivalent to the EU's DOP (Protected Designation of Origin)
  • Strictly defined: area · permitted varieties · minimum alcohol · maximum yield · winemaking methods
  • Mainland Portugal has more than 30 DOCs, such as Douro DOC · Vinho Verde DOC · Dão DOC · Alentejo DOC
  • Under the EU framework it may also be labelled DOP

🥈 IGP (Indicação Geográfica Protegida) = Vinho Regional

  • Equivalent to the EU's IGP (Protected Geographical Indication)
  • Looser than DOC: more varieties and larger areas permitted
  • Portugal has 14 Vinho Regional areas, such as Alentejano · Minho · Duriense
  • Many innovative producers choose IGP labelling to break free of DOC variety restrictions

🥉 Vinho (simple table wine)

  • No regional restriction; blending across regions is allowed
  • The most basic tier, labelled simply "Vinho"

slides.3.question: What tier of Portuguese wine is Vinho Verde?
slides.3.explanation: Vinho Verde is one of Portugal's major DOCs (legally defined appellations), which regulate the area, permitted varieties and winemaking methods. Note: "Vinho Verde" means "green wine" and is not a quality tier but the name of the DOC.
slides.4.title: Label Terms: VR, Reserva, Garrafeira
slides.4.html:
Several common terms on Portuguese labels each carry a clear legal minimum:

  • Vinho Regional (VR): at least 85% of the grapes must come from the stated region; a wide range of varieties is allowed, with a minimum alcohol level
  • Reserva (still wines): alcohol must be at least 0.5% higher than the legal minimum for that DOC/VR (stricter individual DOC rules prevail); for traditional-method sparkling wines, Reserva means ≥ 12 months ageing on the lees in bottle
  • Colheita Seleccionada: alcohol at least 1% higher than the regional legal minimum
  • Garrafeira (vintage-dated DOC/VR only): reds aged ≥ 30 months (including ≥ 12 months in bottle); whites and rosés ≥ 12 months (≥ 6 months in bottle)

Based on data compiled in 2011–2012; where an individual DOC has stricter rules, that DOC's rules apply.
